title: Dysphagia Revealing a Pharyngeal–cervical–brachial Variant of Guillain–Barré Syndrome in Pediatric Cases
case_prompt: A 13-year-old boy with no significant medical history and no recent infections or exposures presented with a 4-day history of dysphagia and dyspnea on a background of low-grade fever and malaise. Twenty-four hours after admission, he developed descending muscle weakness that began in the fingers and hands bilaterally and subsequently progressed to involve the forearms and proximal lower limbs. On examination, he had a normal gait, bilateral upper-limb weakness (2/5) and lower-limb weakness (4/5), preserved deep-tendon reflexes, bulbar muscle involvement, and no sensory deficits. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, electrolytes, and C-reactive protein, were within normal limits. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed a protein level of 0.51 g/L, 2 white cells, and sterile culture, without albuminocytological dissociation. MRI of the complete neuraxis was normal. Electromyography demonstrated an acute pure motor axonal polyneuropathy with markedly slowed conduction velocities in the upper limbs.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. A structural central nervous system process, such as brainstem stroke or malformation, was unlikely — “The magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the complete neurological axis revealed normal findings.”  
2. Botulism was excluded by the lack of characteristic exposure history and absence of ocular or autonomic features — “There was no reported history of honey consumption, iridoplegia, or autonomic dysfunction, ruling out botulism.”  
3. Neuromuscular junction disorders and myopathies were considered but were less consistent due to intact sensation and preserved reflexes — “To differentiate from myasthenia gravis, botulism, and other myopathic disorders, PCB is characterized by the absence of sensory deficits or areflexia.”  
4. Miller Fisher syndrome was unlikely in the absence of ophthalmoplegia or lower-limb involvement — “PCB is defined as ‘pure’ when patients exhibit rapidly progressive oropharyngeal and cervicobrachial weakness accompanied by areflexia/hyporeflexia but without ophthalmoplegia or leg weakness.”
